en.title: The history of medicine
en.summary: Anatomy, anaesthesia, antiseptics and public health in English-speaking medicine.

paragraphs: Modern medicine is only about two hundred years old. In this lesson you will read how doctors learned to see inside the body, to stop pain and to prevent infection, and you will practise the structure it was not until... that.

For centuries doctors treated illness by methods that did little good. William Harvey's description of the circulation of blood in 1628 started a new, scientific approach. The first operation under ether anaesthesia took place in Boston in 1846, and the patient felt no pain. It was not until the 1860s that Joseph Lister, a Scottish surgeon, showed that cleaning wounds and instruments with carbolic acid reduced deaths from infection. In 1854 the London doctor John Snow traced an outbreak of cholera to a water pump in Broad Street, and he persuaded the authorities to remove its handle. Florence Nightingale, whose hospital in the Crimean War saved many lives, used statistics to argue for cleaner hospitals.

paragraphs: **1. It was not until... that.** The sentence stresses how late something happened. See Introduction to Grammar: Sentence structure.

items: **Anaesthesia** (anesthesia in American English) is the loss of feeling for an operation.
**Antiseptic** kills germs on skin and instruments.
**Cholera** is a disease spread by dirty water.

paragraphs: John Snow's map of cholera cases is often called the beginning of modern epidemiology, the study of how diseases spread.
